title: Πρέσβεις ἐπανιόντες
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Achilles answers Phoenix: he has no need of the honour Phoenix offers, he will stay by the ships as long as he lives, and Phoenix is not to grieve him for Agamemnon's sake; let Phoenix sleep in a soft bed, and at dawn they will decide whether to sail or stay. Achilles nods to Patroclus to make the bed, and Ajax tells Odysseus it is time to go: the errand will come to nothing, the army is waiting for the unwelcome news, and Achilles has made his heart savage over one girl when other men take a price for a brother or a son. Achilles grants that Ajax speaks to his liking, but his heart swells whenever he remembers how Agamemnon treated him; he will not think of war until Hector reaches the Myrmidon huts and ships, and there, he thinks, Hector will be stopped. The envoys pour a libation and go; Patroclus has Phoenix's bed made, and Achilles and Patroclus each lie down with a woman. In Agamemnon's hut the chiefs greet the envoys with cups, and Odysseus reports that Achilles will not quench his anger, rejects the gifts, and threatens to sail at dawn. Everyone is silent until Diomedes speaks: Agamemnon should not have begged him, Achilles will fight when his heart and a god move him, and for now they should eat, sleep, and at dawn draw up the army with Agamemnon fighting among the first. The kings approve and go to sleep.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: This is the reply formula: τὸν is ‘him’ (the article as a pronoun), ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ and προσέφη the aorist of προσφημί ‘speak to’, while πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’ is a stock epithet with πόδας as an accusative of respect. Achilles answers Phoenix, whose speech closed at 605. The speech itself begins in the next unit; the edition prints no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
Φοῖνιξ ἄττα γεραιὲ διοτρεφὲς οὔ τί με ταύτης
χρεὼ τιμῆς·
sentences.tr:
Phoinix atta geraie diotrephes ou ti me tautēs
chreō timēs·
sentences.l:
“Phoenix, father, aged one, Zeus-nurtured one, not at all for me of this
honour is there need;
sentences.i: “Father Phoenix, old man, Zeus-nurtured one, I have no need at all of this honour;
sentences.n: Φοῖνιξ ἄττα γεραιὲ διοτρεφές is a chain of vocatives: ἄττα is a respectful word for an older man (‘father’, not a family term), γεραιέ is ‘aged one’ (‘old man’ in the free line), and διοτρεφές ‘Zeus-nurtured one’ is the stock epithet of kings, here given to Phoenix. οὔ τί με … χρεώ is ‘there is no need for me’, i.e. ‘I have no need’: χρεώ (‘need’, with ἐστί understood) takes the accusative of the person and the genitive of the thing, ταύτης τιμῆς ‘of this honour’. The honour is the one Phoenix has just held out in return for yielding (604–605).

sentences.t:
φρονέω δὲ τετιμῆσθαι Διὸς αἴσῃ,
ἥ μ’ ἕξει παρὰ νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν εἰς ὅ κ’ ἀϋτμὴ
ἐν στήθεσσι μένῃ καί μοι φίλα γούνατ’ ὀρώρῃ.
sentences.tr:
phroneō de tetimēsthai Dios aisēi,
hē m’ hexei para nēusi korōnisin eis ho k’ aÿtmē
en stēthessi menēi kai moi phila gounat’ orōrēi.
sentences.l:
but I think myself honoured by the portion of Zeus,
which will hold me by the curved ships for as long as breath
in my chest remains and my dear knees are stirred.
sentences.i: but I count myself honoured by the lot of Zeus, which will keep me by the curved ships for as long as breath stays in my chest and my knees can move.
sentences.n: φρονέω … τετιμῆσθαι is ‘I think (that I am) honoured’, τετιμῆσθαι being the perfect passive infinitive of τιμάω. Διὸς αἴσῃ ‘by the portion of Zeus’: αἶσα is the share a god allots to a man, and the dative gives the means of the honour. ἥ is the relative, with αἴσῃ as its antecedent, and ἕξει is the future of ἔχω ‘hold’. εἰς ὅ κ’ … μένῃ is ‘for as long as’ (literally ‘up to the time when’) with a subjunctive; ἀϋτμή is ‘breath’ and ὀρώρῃ the perfect subjunctive of ὄρνυμι, ‘be stirred, be in motion’. νηυσί is the epic dative plural of ναῦς, and κορωνίσιν ‘curved’ agrees with it. Achilles’ answer to the offer of honour is that he already has a different one.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσι·
sentences.tr: allo de toi ereō, sy d’ eni phresi balleo sēisi·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: Achilles used this very line to Agamemnon at 1.297, where it opened a refusal and a threat; here it opens an instruction to a friend. ἐρέω is the future of ἐρῶ ‘I shall say’, βάλλεο the imperative middle in the epic ending -εο (‘put, lay’), and σῇσι the epic dative plural of σός ‘your own’.

sentences.t:
μή μοι σύγχει θυμὸν ὀδυρόμενος καὶ ἀχεύων
Ἀτρεΐδῃ ἥρωϊ φέρων χάριν·
sentences.tr:
mē moi synchei thymon odyromenos kai acheuōn
Atreïdēi hērōï pherōn charin·
sentences.l:
do not for me confound my heart, lamenting and grieving,
to Atreus’-son the hero bringing a favour;
sentences.i: do not confuse my heart with lamenting and grieving, bringing a favour to the hero, the son of Atreus;
sentences.n: μή … σύγχει is a prohibition with the present imperative, ‘do not go on confusing’, from συγχέω ‘pour together, throw into confusion’; μοι is a dative of interest (‘on me’). ὀδυρόμενος καὶ ἀχεύων ‘lamenting and grieving’ describes what Phoenix has been doing, in tears (9.432–433). Ἀτρεΐδῃ ἥρωϊ φέρων χάριν is ‘bringing favour to Atreus’-son the hero’: ἥρως here is only a title of respect, ‘the hero’, and Achilles uses it for Agamemnon without naming him.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε χρὴ
τὸν φιλέειν, ἵνα μή μοι ἀπέχθηαι φιλέοντι.
sentences.tr:
oude ti se chrē
ton phileein, hina mē moi apechthēai phileonti.
sentences.l:
and not at all ought you
him to love, so that you not become hateful to me who love you.
sentences.i: and you ought not to love him, so that you do not become hateful to me, who love you.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τί σε χρή … φιλέειν is ‘nor ought you at all to love’: χρή ‘it is necessary’ takes the accusative of the person and an infinitive, and φιλέειν is the uncontracted infinitive (Attic φιλεῖν). τόν is ‘him’ (Agamemnon), the article as a pronoun. ἵνα μὴ … ἀπέχθηαι is a negative purpose clause, with ἀπέχθηαι the aorist subjunctive of ἀπεχθάνομαι ‘become hateful’ in its open epic form (Attic ἀπέχθῃ); φιλέοντι is a dative participle agreeing with μοι, ‘to me who love you’.

sentences.t: καλόν τοι σὺν ἐμοὶ τὸν κήδειν ὅς κ’ ἐμὲ κήδῃ·
sentences.tr: kalon toi syn emoi ton kēdein hos k’ eme kēdēi·
sentences.l: Fine it is for you, along with me, him to distress who may distress me;
sentences.i: It is a fine thing for you to join me in distressing the man who distresses me;
sentences.n: τοι is ‘to you’ and σὺν ἐμοί ‘with me’. κήδειν is the active infinitive of κήδω ‘distress, trouble’, and κήδῃ (in ὃς κ’ ἐμὲ κήδῃ) the active subjunctive in a general relative clause; this is not the middle κήδομαι ‘care for’, which looks similar. τὸν is ‘him’, the article as a pronoun. The saying is the old rule of friends and enemies: those who hurt me you should hurt with me.

sentences.t: ἶσον ἐμοὶ βασίλευε καὶ ἥμισυ μείρεο τιμῆς.
sentences.tr: ison emoi basileue kai hēmisy meireo timēs.
sentences.l: Equally with me be king, and take half of the honour.
sentences.i: Be king beside me as my equal, and take half of the honour.
sentences.n: ἶσον ἐμοί is ‘equally with me’ (ἶσον adverbial, with the dative). βασίλευε is the present imperative of βασιλεύω ‘be king’, and μείρεο the imperative of μείρομαι ‘receive as one’s share’, in the epic ending -εο, with ἥμισυ ‘half’ as its object and τιμῆς ‘of the honour’ in the genitive. What Achilles offers Phoenix is half of his own standing, in place of the honour that Agamemnon’s gifts would buy.

sentences.t:
οὗτοι δ’ ἀγγελέουσι, σὺ δ’ αὐτόθι λέξεο μίμνων
εὐνῇ ἔνι μαλακῇ·
sentences.tr:
houtoi d’ angeleousi, sy d’ autothi lexeo mimnōn
eunēi eni malakēi·
sentences.l:
These will carry the news, and you here lie down, staying
in a soft bed;
sentences.i: These men will carry the news; you stay here and lie down in a soft bed;
sentences.n: οὗτοι ‘these men’ are the envoys who are about to leave. ἀγγελέουσι is the epic future of ἀγγέλλω ‘carry word’; σὺ δ’ αὐτόθι is ‘but you, here (on the spot)’. λέξεο is the aorist imperative middle of λέγομαι ‘lie down’, in the epic ending -εο, and μίμνων ‘staying’; εὐνῇ ἔνι μαλακῇ is ‘in a soft bed’, with ἔνι (= ἐνί ‘in’) set after its noun.

sentences.t:
ἅμα δ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι
φρασσόμεθ’ ἤ κε νεώμεθ’ ἐφ’ ἡμέτερ’ ἦ κε μένωμεν.
sentences.tr:
hama d’ ēoi phainomenēphi
phrassometh’ ē ke neōmeth’ eph’ hēmeter’ ē ke menōmen.
sentences.l:
and with dawn appearing
we shall take counsel whether we go back to our own, or stay.”
sentences.i: and at first light we shall take counsel whether to go back to our own homes or to stay.”
sentences.n: ἅμα δ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι is ‘and with dawn appearing’, a formula for ‘at first light’; ἠοῖ is the dative of ἠώς ‘dawn’ and φαινομένηφι ‘appearing’ has the old ending -φι. φρασσόμεθα is the future of φράζομαι ‘take counsel, consider’. ἤ κε νεώμεθ’ … ἦ κε μένωμεν is ‘whether we go back … or stay’, a double question with subjunctives (νεώμεθα from νέομαι ‘go back’); ἡμέτερα is the neuter plural ‘our own (things)’, here our own country and homes. Achilles does not say yes or no: the decision waits for the morning.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ Πατρόκλῳ ὅ γ’ ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσε σιωπῇ
Φοίνικι στορέσαι πυκινὸν λέχος, ὄφρα τάχιστα
ἐκ κλισίης νόστοιο μεδοίατο·
sentences.tr:
ē kai Patroklōi ho g’ ep’ ophrysi neuse siōpēi
Phoiniki storesai pykinon lechos, ophra tachista
ek klisiēs nostoio medoiato·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and nodded with his brows to Patroclus, in silence, to spread a solid bed for Phoenix, so that they could think as soon as possible of going home from the hut;
sentences.n: ἦ καί is ‘he spoke, and’, the usual way of adding a gesture to a speech; ὅ γ’ is Achilles, and ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσε is ‘nodded with his brows’. The nod is silent (σιωπῇ) and carries an order: Φοίνικι στορέσαι πυκινὸν λέχος is ‘to spread a solid bed for Phoenix’ (στορέσαι the aorist infinitive of στόρνυμι; Φοίνικι a dative of the person served). ὄφρα τάχιστα … μεδοίατο is a purpose clause, the present optative of μέδομαι ‘be mindful of’ with the genitive νόστοιο ‘their return’, and ἐκ κλισίης ‘from the hut’. The unnamed ‘they’ are the other envoys, who can go once Phoenix is settled.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἄρ’ Αἴας
ἀντίθεος Τελαμωνιάδης μετὰ μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ ar’ Aias
antitheos Telamōniadēs meta mython eeipe·
sentences.l:
and among them Ajax,
godlike, son of Telamon, a speech spoke:
sentences.i: and godlike Ajax, son of Telamon, spoke among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is ‘to them’ (the article as a pronoun), and μετὰ … ἔειπε is a tmesis, ‘spoke among’, with ἔειπε an aorist with doubled ε (= Attic εἶπε); μῦθον is the object, ‘a speech’. Ἀντίθεος ‘godlike’ is the epithet of Ajax, and Τελαμωνιάδης a patronymic, ‘son of Telamon’, built like Ἀτρεΐδης.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ
ἴομεν·
sentences.tr:
diogenes Laertiadē polymēchan’ Odysseu
iomen·
sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
let us go;
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, let us go;
sentences.n: The whole vocative is a formula for Odysseus: διογενές ‘Zeus-born’ (a title of rank, not a claim of descent), Λαερτιάδη ‘son of Laertes’ (a patronymic in the vocative) and πολυμήχαν’ (πολυμήχανε) ‘of many devices’. ἴομεν is the epic hortative ‘let us go’ (Attic ἴωμεν). Ajax speaks to Odysseus as the leader of the embassy.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ μοι δοκέει μύθοιο τελευτὴ
τῇδέ γ’ ὁδῷ κρανέεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
ou gar moi dokeei mythoio teleutē
tēide g’ hodōi kraneesthai·
sentences.l:
for not to me does it seem that the end of the speech
by this way will be accomplished;
sentences.i: for I do not think that our talk will be brought to its end along this road;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ μοι δοκέει is ‘for it does not seem to me’, with the infinitive κρανέεσθαι, the future (passive in sense) of κραίνω ‘accomplish’ in its epic form. μύθοιο τελευτή is ‘the end (the outcome) of the talk’, with the epic genitive in -οιο; and τῇδέ γ’ ὁδῷ ‘by this way’ is a dative of way. ὁδός is a road, here the course the embassy has taken: Ajax says this approach has failed.

sentences.t:
ἀπαγγεῖλαι δὲ τάχιστα
χρὴ μῦθον Δαναοῖσι καὶ οὐκ ἀγαθόν περ ἐόντα
οἵ που νῦν ἕαται ποτιδέγμενοι.
sentences.tr:
apangeilai de tachista
chrē mython Danaoisi kai ouk agathon per eonta
hoi pou nyn heatai potidegmenoi.
sentences.l:
and to report most quickly
is necessary the word to the Danaans, even though it is not good,
who perhaps now sit waiting.
sentences.i: and we must report the word to the Danaans as quickly as we can, even though it is not a good one; they are probably sitting there now, waiting.
sentences.n: ἀπαγγεῖλαι is the aorist infinitive of ἀπαγγέλλω ‘report’, and χρή ‘it is necessary’ governs it with ‘us’ understood; μῦθον is ‘word’ in the sense of a message. οὐκ ἀγαθόν περ ἐόντα is ‘though it is not good’ (περ makes it concessive; ἐόντα is the epic participle of εἰμί, Attic ὄντα, agreeing with μῦθον). The relative οἵ points back to Δαναοῖσι. ἕαται is the Ionic third plural of ἧμαι ‘sit’ (Attic κάθηνται) and ποτιδέγμενοι ‘waiting’ a participle of προσδέχομαι with ποτί for πρός; που ‘I suppose’ softens the claim.

sentences.t:
αὐτάρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἄγριον ἐν στήθεσσι θέτο μεγαλήτορα θυμὸν
σχέτλιος,
sentences.tr:
autar Achilleus
agrion en stēthessi theto megalētora thymon
schetlios,
sentences.l:
but Achilles
a wild, great-spirited heart in his chest has set,
cruel one,
sentences.i: But Achilles has set a wild, great-spirited heart in his chest, the cruel one,
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns from the waiting army to Achilles. θέτο is the aorist middle of τίθημι, without augment, ‘has put (for himself)’; its object is θυμὸν, with ἄγριον ‘wild’ (the word for untamed beasts and country) and μεγαλήτορα ‘great-spirited’ in the stock phrase, an odd pair that the translation keeps. ἐν στήθεσσι ‘in his chest’ has the epic dative plural. σχέτλιος ‘cruel one’ is a nominative reproach hung on Ἀχιλλεύς.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ μετατρέπεται φιλότητος ἑταίρων
τῆς ᾗ μιν παρὰ νηυσὶν ἐτίομεν ἔξοχον ἄλλων
νηλής·
sentences.tr:
oude metatrepetai philotētos hetairōn
tēs hēi min para nēusin etiomen exochon allōn
nēlēs·
sentences.i: and he gives no thought to the friendship of his companions, in which we honoured him beside the ships above all others, the pitiless one;
sentences.n: οὐδὲ μετατρέπεται is ‘nor does he turn to regard’, and the genitive φιλότητος ἑταίρων ‘the friendship of his companions’ is what he fails to regard. τῆς picks φιλότητος up (‘that friendship’), and ᾗ is the relative ‘in which, with which’; ἐτίομεν is the imperfect of τίω ‘honour’. ἔξοχον ἄλλων is ‘above all others’, with ἔξοχον adverbial; the phrase comes again at 641. νηλής ‘pitiless one’ is the second reproach after σχέτλιος.

sentences.t:
καὶ μέν τίς τε κασιγνήτοιο φονῆος
ποινὴν ἢ οὗ παιδὸς ἐδέξατο τεθνηῶτος·
sentences.tr:
kai men tis te kasignētoio phonēos
poinēn ē hou paidos edexato tethnēōtos·
sentences.l:
And indeed someone, of a brother’s slayer,
requital, or of his own child, dead, accepted;
sentences.i: And yet a man accepts requital from his brother’s slayer, or for his own dead child;
sentences.n: The aorist ἐδέξατο is gnomic: it states what men do, so the English says ‘accepts’; τίς τε adds the same general colour. ποινή ‘requital’ is the price paid to a family for a killing. The construction is loose: κασιγνήτοιο φονῆος is ‘a brother’s slayer’ (φονῆος the epic genitive of φονεύς), and οὗ παιδὸς … τεθνηῶτος ‘his own child, dead’; the sense is a price taken for a killed brother or child. οὗ is the possessive ὅς ‘his own’, genitive, agreeing with παιδός, and τεθνηῶτος a perfect participle of θνῄσκω.

sentences.t:
καί ῥ’ ὃ μὲν ἐν δήμῳ μένει αὐτοῦ πόλλ’ ἀποτίσας,
τοῦ δέ τ’ ἐρητύεται κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
ποινὴν δεξαμένῳ·
sentences.tr:
kai rh’ ho men en dēmōi menei autou poll’ apotisas,
tou de t’ erētyetai kradiē kai thymos agēnōr
poinēn dexamenōi·
sentences.i: and the slayer stays right there among the people, having paid a great deal, while the heart and proud spirit of the other are held back, now that he has accepted requital;
sentences.n: καί ῥ’ ὃ μὲν … τοῦ δέ is ‘and so he … but of the other’: ὃ μέν is the slayer, who stays in his place (αὐτοῦ ‘right there’) among the people, πόλλ’ ἀποτίσας ‘having paid much’ (aorist participle of ἀποτίνω ‘pay back’). τοῦ is the man who lost kin; ἐρητύεται is passive, ‘is held back’, and κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ is ‘heart and manly spirit’ (the adjective, ‘manly’ or ‘proud’, is rendered ‘proud’ in the free line). ποινὴν δεξαμένῳ is a dative participle, ‘to him who has accepted requital’, attached loosely to τοῦ.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ ἄληκτόν τε κακόν τε
θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι θεοὶ θέσαν εἵνεκα κούρης
οἴης·
sentences.tr:
soi d’ alēkton te kakon te
thymon eni stēthessi theoi thesan heineka kourēs
oiēs·
sentences.i: But in your chest the gods have put a relentless, evil heart, for the sake of one girl alone;
sentences.n: σοὶ δέ turns from the avenger to Achilles, with the emphasis on ‘you’. ἄληκτον τε κακόν τε are two adjectives joined by τε … τε, ‘both relentless and evil’, agreeing with θυμόν in the next line; ἄληκτος is formed from ἀ- and λήγω ‘cease’. θέσαν is the aorist of τίθημι without augment (= ἔθεσαν). εἵνεκα (= ἕνεκα) κούρης οἴης is ‘for the sake of one girl alone’, with οἴης the epic feminine genitive of οἶος ‘alone’. The girl is Briseis, whom Ajax does not name.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ τοι ἑπτὰ παρίσχομεν ἔξοχ’ ἀρίστας,
ἄλλά τε πόλλ’ ἐπὶ τῇσι·
sentences.tr:
nyn de toi hepta parischomen exoch’ aristas,
alla te poll’ epi tēisi·
sentences.l:
but now to you we furnish seven, above all others the best,
and other things, many, in addition to them;
sentences.i: But now we offer you seven women, the best above all others, and many other things besides them;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but now’ sets the offer against the grievance. παρίσχομεν is the epic present of παρέχω ‘furnish, offer’. ἑπτά … ἀρίστας is ‘seven, the best’: the noun is left out, and the translation supplies ‘women’ from Agamemnon’s offer at 9.128 (seven women of Lesbos). ἔξοχ’ (ἔξοχα) is the adverb ‘above all others’, strengthening ἀρίστας. ἄλλά τε πόλλ’ ἐπὶ τῇσι is ‘and many other things in addition to them’, with ἐπί ‘besides’ and τῇσι the epic dative plural of the article as a pronoun.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ ἵλαον ἔνθεο θυμόν,
αἴδεσσαι δὲ μέλαθρον·
sentences.tr:
sy d’ hilaon entheo thymon,
aidessai de melathron·
sentences.l:
but you, a gracious heart put in yourself,
and respect the roof;
sentences.i: Now put a gracious heart in yourself, and show respect for the roof;
sentences.n: σὺ δ’ … ἔνθεο: ἔνθεο is the aorist imperative middle of ἐντίθημι ‘put in’, so ‘put (in yourself) a gracious heart’. ἵλαον ‘gracious’ is the epic form of the word that is ἵλεως in Attic. αἴδεσσαι is the aorist imperative middle of αἰδέομαι, here ‘show respect to’ rather than ‘be ashamed’. μέλαθρον ‘roof’ stands for the hut and for the host’s duty to those under it, as the next unit says.

sentences.t:
ὑπωρόφιοι δέ τοί εἰμεν
πληθύος ἐκ Δαναῶν, μέμαμεν δέ τοι ἔξοχον ἄλλων
κήδιστοί τ’ ἔμεναι καὶ φίλτατοι ὅσσοι Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr:
hypōrophioi de toi eimen
plēthyos ek Danaōn, memamen de toi exochon allōn
kēdistoi t’ emenai kai philtatoi hossoi Achaioi.
sentences.i: for we are under your roof, men out of the throng of the Danaans, and we are eager, above all others, to be the closest and the dearest to you of all the Achaeans there are.”
sentences.n: ὑπωρόφιοι ‘under (your) roof’ is built from ὑπό and ὄροφος ‘roof’, and is why the host owes them respect; πληθύος ἐκ Δαναῶν is ‘out of the throng of the Danaans’. μέμαμεν is a perfect with present sense, ‘we are eager’; ἔμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί. κήδιστοι is a superlative of κῆδος ‘connection, care’ and means ‘closest-tied’ (the Odyssey uses it of kin by marriage and of a closest companion); ὅσσοι Ἀχαιοί is ‘as many as are Achaeans’, ‘of all the Achaeans there are’. ἔξοχον ἄλλων ‘above all others’ repeats 631, now as an appeal.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at 606: Achilles now answers Ajax.

sentences.t:
Αἶαν διογενὲς Τελαμώνιε κοίρανε λαῶν
πάντά τί μοι κατὰ θυμὸν ἐείσαο μυθήσασθαι·
sentences.tr:
Aian diogenes Telamōnie koirane laōn
panta ti moi kata thymon eeisao mythēsasthai·
sentences.l:
“Ajax, Zeus-sprung, Telamonian, ruler of the people,
everything for me according to my heart you seem to have said;
sentences.i: “Zeus-born Ajax, Telamonian, ruler of the people, everything you have said seems to me to be after my own heart;
sentences.n: Αἶαν διογενὲς Τελαμώνιε κοίρανε λαῶν is the vocative Hector used to Ajax at 7.234: Αἶαν is the vocative of Αἴας, διογενές ‘Zeus-born’, Τελαμώνιε ‘Telamonian’, κοίρανε λαῶν ‘ruler of the people’. πάντά τί μοι κατὰ θυμὸν ἐείσαο μυθήσασθαι is ‘you seem to me to have said everything after my heart’: ἐείσαο is the second person singular aorist middle of εἴδομαι ‘seem’, with the infinitive μυθήσασθαι ‘to say’, and κατὰ θυμόν ‘according to my heart’ means ‘to my mind’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι οἰδάνεται κραδίη χόλῳ ὁππότε κείνων
μνήσομαι ὥς μ’ ἀσύφηλον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔρεξεν
Ἀτρεΐδης ὡς εἴ τιν’ ἀτίμητον μετανάστην.
sentences.tr:
alla moi oidanetai kradiē cholōi hoppote keinōn
mnēsomai hōs m’ asyphēlon en Argeioisin erexen
Atreïdēs hōs ei tin’ atimēton metanastēn.
sentences.l:
but my heart swells with anger whenever of those things
I think, how disgracefully among the Argives me he treated,
Atreus’-son, as if some unhonoured migrant.
sentences.i: But my heart swells with anger whenever I remember those things, how the son of Atreus treated me disgracefully among the Argives, as though I were some unhonoured migrant.
sentences.n: ἀλλά marks the contrast with the previous unit: Ajax speaks well, but Achilles’ heart is another matter. οἰδάνεται is the present of οἰδάνω ‘swell’, and χόλῳ ‘with anger’ is a dative of cause. ὁππότε κείνων μνήσομαι is ‘whenever I think of those things’, with μνήσομαι (a future, or a short-vowel subjunctive of μιμνῄσκομαι) taking the genitive. ἀσύφηλον is a rare word whose exact sense is not known; ‘disgracefully’ is the sense the context supports. ἔρεξεν is the aorist of ῥέζω ‘do, treat’, and ὡς εἴ τιν’ … μετανάστην is ‘as (he would treat) some migrant’, a settler from elsewhere with no rights, ἀτίμητον ‘unhonoured’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς ἔρχεσθε καὶ ἀγγελίην ἀπόφασθε·
sentences.tr: all’ hymeis erchesthe kai angeliēn apophasthe·
sentences.l: but you go, and the news declare;
sentences.i: But as for you, go and declare the news;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὑμεῖς is ‘but you (all)’. ἔρχεσθε is a present imperative, and ἀπόφασθε an aorist imperative middle from ἀπόφημι ‘declare, speak out’; ἀγγελίην is ‘news’, the message Achilles wants carried back.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πρὶν πολέμοιο μεδήσομαι αἱματόεντος
πρίν γ’ υἱὸν Πριάμοιο δαΐφρονος Ἕκτορα δῖον
Μυρμιδόνων ἐπί τε κλισίας καὶ νῆας ἱκέσθαι
κτείνοντ’ Ἀργείους, κατά τε σμῦξαι πυρὶ νῆας.
sentences.tr:
ou gar prin polemoio medēsomai haimatoentos
prin g’ huion Priamoio daïphronos Hektora dion
Myrmidonōn epi te klisias kai nēas hikesthai
kteinont’ Argeious, kata te smyxai pyri nēas.
sentences.l:
for not before will I think of bloody war
before the son of Priam, wise-minded, Hector, heavenly,
to the huts and the ships of the Myrmidons has come,
killing Argives, and burned the ships down with fire.
sentences.i: For I will not give a thought to bloody war until the son of wise-hearted Priam, heavenly Hector, has come to the huts and ships of the Myrmidons, killing Argives, and burned the ships down with fire.
sentences.n: οὐ γὰρ πρὶν … πρίν γ’ … ἱκέσθαι is ‘for not before … until’, πρίν taking the infinitive with Ἕκτορα as its subject; μεδήσομαι is the future of μέδομαι ‘be mindful of’ with the genitive πολέμοιο, so ‘I shall not give thought to war’, that is, he will not fight. δαΐφρονος is the stock epithet of Priam, traditionally ‘wise-minded’ though ‘fierce’ is also argued, and δῖον ‘heavenly’ goes with Ἕκτορα. Μυρμιδόνων is the genitive of the Myrmidons, Achilles’ men, for both κλισίας and νῆας; κτείνοντ’ is an accusative participle agreeing with Ἕκτορα. κατά τε σμῦξαι is a tmesis for the aorist infinitive of κατασμύχω, ‘burn down’, with πυρί ‘with fire’.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ τοι τῇ ἐμῇ κλισίῃ καὶ νηῒ μελαίνῃ
Ἕκτορα καὶ μεμαῶτα μάχης σχήσεσθαι ὀΐω.
sentences.tr:
amphi de toi tēi emēi klisiēi kai nēï melainēi
Hektora kai memaōta machēs schēsesthai oïō.
sentences.l:
And about this hut of mine and my black ship
Hector, eager though he is, from battle will hold himself back, I think.”
sentences.i: And I think that Hector, eager though he is, will hold himself back from battle around my hut and my black ship.”
sentences.n: ἀμφί … κλισίῃ καὶ νηῒ μελαίνῃ is ‘about my hut and black ship’ (ἀμφί with the dative); τοι is ‘I tell you’, and τῇ ἐμῇ ‘this … of mine’. Ἕκτορα … σχήσεσθαι ὀΐω is ‘I think Hector will restrain himself’: ὀΐω is ‘I think’, and σχήσεσθαι the future infinitive middle of ἔχω, with μάχης a genitive of separation, ‘from battle’; μεμαῶτα ‘though eager’ is a participle agreeing with Ἕκτορα. Achilles sets the limit of his refusal: only at his own hut and ship will he fight.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δὲ ἕκαστος ἑλὼν δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον
σπείσαντες παρὰ νῆας ἴσαν πάλιν·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi de hekastos helōn depas amphikypellon
speisantes para nēas isan palin·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they, each one taking a double cup,
having poured a libation, went back along the ships;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and each of them took a double cup, poured a libation, and went back along the ships;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech; οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the envoys. δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is the ‘double cup’, and ἑλών (‘taking’) and σπείσαντες (‘having poured a libation’) are aorist participles. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ (= ᾖσαν), παρὰ νῆας ‘along the ships’, πάλιν ‘back’. The libation is the formal end of a visit; ἕκαστος ‘each’ is singular, with a plural verb.

sentences.t: ἦρχε δ’ Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.tr: ērche d’ Odysseus.
sentences.l: and led Odysseus.
sentences.i: and Odysseus led the way.
sentences.n: ἦρχε is the imperfect of ἄρχω ‘lead the way’; Odysseus goes first, as the spokesman of the embassy.

sentences.t:
Πάτροκλος δ’ ἑτάροισιν ἰδὲ δμωῇσι κέλευσε
Φοίνικι στορέσαι πυκινὸν λέχος ὅττι τάχιστα.
sentences.tr:
Patroklos d’ hetaroisin ide dmōēisi keleuse
Phoiniki storesai pykinon lechos hotti tachista.
sentences.l:
And Patroclus to his companions and to the maidservants gave orders
to spread for Phoenix a solid bed as quickly as possible.
sentences.i: And Patroclus ordered his companions and the maids to spread a solid bed for Phoenix as quickly as they could.
sentences.n: Patroclus carries out the nod of 620–621. ἑτάροισιν ἰδὲ δμωῇσι is ‘to his companions and to the maidservants’ (ἑταῖροι are his own men, δμωαί the women servants of the hut; ἰδέ is ‘and’), and κέλευσε takes the dative with an infinitive, ‘gave orders to spread’. Φοίνικι στορέσαι πυκινὸν λέχος is the same phrase as at 621; ὅττι τάχιστα is ‘as quickly as possible’ (ὅττι is ὅτι with the doubled consonant).

sentences.t:
αἳ δ’ ἐπιπειθόμεναι στόρεσαν λέχος ὡς ἐκέλευσε
κώεά τε ῥῆγός τε λίνοιό τε λεπτὸν ἄωτον.
sentences.tr:
hai d’ epipeithomenai storesan lechos hōs ekeleuse
kōea te rhēgos te linoio te lepton aōton.
sentences.l:
And they, obeying, spread the bed as he ordered,
fleeces and a rug and the fine nap of linen.
sentences.i: The maids obeyed and spread the bed as he had ordered, with fleeces and a rug and the fine nap of linen.
sentences.n: αἳ δ’ is ‘and they’, the maidservants, and ἐπιπειθόμεναι ‘obeying’ a participle of ἐπιπείθομαι; στόρεσαν is the aorist of στόρνυμι without augment. The bedding is listed in apposition to λέχος: κώεα ‘fleeces’, ῥῆγος ‘a rug’ (a woollen covering), and λίνοιο … ἄωτον ‘the nap of linen’. ἄωτος means a tuft, the nap or finest part of a cloth; what exactly was laid down (the soft top layer of fine linen) is only inferred.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ὃ γέρων κατέλεκτο καὶ ἠῶ δῖαν ἔμιμνεν.
sentences.tr: enth’ ho gerōn katelekto kai ēō dian emimnen.
sentences.l: There the old man lay down and waited for heavenly dawn.
sentences.i: There the old man lay down and waited for heavenly dawn.
sentences.n: ὃ γέρων is ‘the old man’ (the article as a pronoun), Phoenix. κατέλεκτο is the root aorist of καταλέγομαι ‘lay down’, without the -σα- of ἐλέξατο at 666, and ἔμιμνεν the imperfect of μίμνω, ‘waited for’; ἠῶ δῖαν is ‘heavenly dawn’, with δῖος as the stock epithet.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς εὗδε μυχῷ κλισίης εὐπήκτου·
sentences.tr: autar Achilleus heude mychōi klisiēs eupēktou·
sentences.l: But Achilles slept in the innermost part of the well-framed hut;
sentences.i: Achilles slept in the innermost corner of his well-framed hut;
sentences.n: μυχῷ is the dative of μυχός ‘innermost part’, a dative of place without a preposition. κλισίης εὐπήκτου is ‘of the well-framed hut’ (εὔπηκτος from εὖ and πήγνυμι ‘fix, fit together’), and εὗδε the imperfect of εὕδω ‘sleep’.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρα παρκατέλεκτο γυνή, τὴν Λεσβόθεν ἦγε,
Φόρβαντος θυγάτηρ Διομήδη καλλιπάρῃος.
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ara parkatelekto gynē, tēn Lesbothen ēge,
Phorbantos thygatēr Diomēdē kalliparēios.
sentences.l:
and beside him lay a woman, whom from Lesbos he had brought,
Diomede, daughter of Phorbas, fair-cheeked.
sentences.i: and beside him lay a woman he had brought from Lesbos, Diomede, the daughter of Phorbas, fair-cheeked.
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘him’ (Achilles). παρκατέλεκτο is παρακατέλεκτο with the final α of παρα- dropped, the aorist of παρακαταλέγομαι ‘lie down beside’. γυνή ‘a woman’ is explained by the apposition in the next line. Λεσβόθεν is ‘from Lesbos’ (the suffix -θεν ‘from’). Διομήδη is the woman’s own name, the feminine form, not the warrior Διομήδης; καλλιπάρῃος ‘fair-cheeked’ is the stock epithet.

sentences.t: Πάτροκλος δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐλέξατο·
sentences.tr: Patroklos d’ heterōthen elexato·
sentences.l: And Patroclus lay down on the other side;
sentences.i: Patroclus lay down on the other side;
sentences.n: ἑτέρωθεν is ‘from the other side’, here ‘on the other side (of the hut)’, and ἐλέξατο the s-aorist of λέγομαι ‘lay down’.

sentences.t:
πὰρ δ’ ἄρα καὶ τῷ
Ἶφις ἐΰζωνος, τήν οἱ πόρε δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
Σκῦρον ἑλὼν αἰπεῖαν Ἐνυῆος πτολίεθρον.
sentences.tr:
par d’ ara kai tōi
Iphis eÿzōnos, tēn hoi pore dios Achilleus
Skyron helōn aipeian Enyēos ptoliethron.
sentences.l:
and beside him too
Iphis, well-girdled, whom to him gave heavenly Achilles,
having taken steep Scyros, the city of Enyeus.
sentences.i: and beside him lay well-girdled Iphis, whom heavenly Achilles gave him when he took steep Scyros, the city of Enyeus.
sentences.n: πὰρ δ’ ἄρα καὶ τῷ is ‘and beside him too’, with πάρ for παρά, the verb of lying down understood from the last unit; τῷ is Patroclus. Ἶφις is a woman’s name, and ἐΰζωνος ‘well-girdled’ the stock epithet. τήν οἱ πόρε is ‘whom he gave him’ (οἱ ‘to him’, πόρε the aorist of an old verb ‘give’, unaugmented). Σκῦρον ἑλών is ‘having taken Scyros’; αἰπεῖαν is feminine and agrees with Σκῦρον (the island), and πτολίεθρον ‘city’ stands in apposition. Ἐνυῆος is the epic genitive of Ἐνυεύς, the man whose city it was.

sentences.t: οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ κλισίῃσιν ἐν Ἀτρεΐδαο γένοντο.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ hote dē klisiēisin en Atreïdao genonto.
sentences.l: And when they had come to be in the huts of Atreus’-son,
sentences.i: When they reached the huts of the son of Atreus,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ὅτε δή is ‘and when’, with οἳ the envoys. κλισίῃσιν ἐν Ἀτρεΐδαο is ‘in the huts of Atreus’-son’, the epic genitive Ἀτρεΐδαο for Agamemnon, and γένοντο is the unaugmented aorist of γίγνομαι, ‘came to be’. The same line stands at 7.313, where the sentence goes on with a comma; here the edition ends it with a full stop, but the construction runs on into the next unit, where the main verb is.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν ἄρα χρυσέοισι κυπέλλοις υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
δειδέχατ’ ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος ἀνασταδόν, ἔκ τ’ ἐρέοντο·
sentences.tr:
tous men ara chryseoisi kypellois huies Achaiōn
deidechat’ allothen allos anastadon, ek t’ ereonto·
sentences.l:
Them then in golden cups the sons of the Achaeans
pledged, one from one side, another from another, standing up, and asked out;
sentences.i: The sons of the Achaeans rose and pledged them in golden cups, one here and another there, and put questions to them;
sentences.n: τοὺς μὲν ἄρα is ‘them then’, the envoys. δειδέχατ’ (δειδέχατο) is the third plural of the old verb δείδεγμαι ‘greet with a cup, pledge’ (the third singular δείδεκτο stands at 9.224; compare Iliad 4.4); ἀνασταδόν is ‘standing up’, rising to greet them. ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is ‘one from one side, another from another’, and ἔκ τ’ ἐρέοντο is ἐξερέοντο split by tmesis, ‘asked out’, i.e. questioned them. The greeting is with golden cups, the host’s honour to the envoys.

sentences.t: πρῶτος δ’ ἐξερέεινεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: prōtos d’ exereeinen anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: and first questioned the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: First of all Agamemnon, lord of men, questioned them:
sentences.n: ἐξερέεινεν is the imperfect of ἐξερεείνω ‘question closely’; πρῶτος ‘first’ is the subject’s predicate, ‘first of all’. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν is ‘lord of men’, the stock epithet.

sentences.l:
“Come, tell me, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans,
is he indeed willing to ward off from the ships the hostile fire,
or has he refused, and does anger still hold his great-spirited heart?”
sentences.i: “Come, tell me, much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans: is he willing to ward the hostile fire off the ships, or has he refused, and does anger still hold his great-spirited heart?”
sentences.n: εἴπ’ ἄγε μ’ is ‘come, tell me’ (εἰπέ and μοι, each elided), then the vocative ὦ πολύαιν’ Ὀδυσεῦ μέγα κῦδος Ἀχαιῶν, ‘much-praised Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans’. ἤ ῥ’ ἐθέλει … ἦ ἀπέειπε is a double question, ‘is he willing … or has he refused?’: ἀλεξέμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἀλέξω ‘ward off’, with νήεσσιν ‘from the ships’ and δήϊον πῦρ ‘hostile fire’, and ἀπέειπε the aorist of ἀπεῖπον, ‘refused’ (not the ‘delivered’ of ἀγγελίην ἀπέειπε at 7.416). χόλος … ἔχει μεγαλήτορα θυμόν is ‘anger holds his great-spirited heart’, with the epithet of 629.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe polytlas dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply formula known from the Odyssey: αὖτε ‘in turn’, προσέειπε ‘addressed’, πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’ the stock epithets of Odysseus. Odysseus answers Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον
κεῖνός γ’ οὐκ ἐθέλει σβέσσαι χόλον, ἀλλ’ ἔτι μᾶλλον
πιμπλάνεται μένεος, σὲ δ’ ἀναίνεται ἠδὲ σὰ δῶρα.
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē kydiste anax andrōn Agamemnon
keinos g’ ouk ethelei sbessai cholon, all’ eti mallon
pimplanetai meneos, se d’ anainetai ēde sa dōra.
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, most glorious, lord of men, Agamemnon,
that man is not willing to quench his anger, but still the more
is filled with fury, and rejects you and your gifts.
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, he is unwilling to quench his anger, but is filled with still more fury, and he rejects you and your gifts.
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον is the formal address Nestor used at 2.434. κεῖνός γ’ is ‘that man’, Achilles, and σβέσσαι the aorist infinitive of σβέννυμι ‘quench’. πιμπλάνεται is a lengthened present of πίμπλημι, ‘is filled’, with the genitive μένεος ‘with fury’ (μένος of anger is ‘fury’). ἀναίνεται is ‘rejects’, with σέ ‘you’ and σὰ δῶρα ‘your gifts’ joined by ἠδέ ‘and’.

sentences.t:
αὐτόν σε φράζεσθαι ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἄνωγεν
ὅππως κεν νῆάς τε σαῷς καὶ λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr:
auton se phrazesthai en Argeioisin anōgen
hoppōs ken nēas te saōis kai laon Achaiōn·
sentences.l:
You yourself to take counsel among the Argives he bade,
how you may save the ships and the people of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: He bade you yourself take counsel, among the Argives, how you may save the ships and the troops of the Achaeans;
sentences.n: αὐτόν σε φράζεσθαι ἄνωγεν is ‘he bade you yourself take counsel’: ἄνωγεν is the old perfect ἄνωγα ‘I bid’ with a past ending, and φράζεσθαι the infinitive of φράζομαι ‘take counsel’. ὅππως κεν is the epic spelling of ὅπως, ‘how’, with κεν and the subjunctive σαῷς, the second person singular of σαόω ‘save’ (Attic σῴζῃς). The tone is pointed: Achilles tells Agamemnon to find his own way to save the army.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἠπείλησεν ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι
νῆας ἐϋσσέλμους ἅλαδ’ ἑλκέμεν ἀμφιελίσσας.
sentences.tr:
autos d’ ēpeilēsen ham’ ēoi phainomenēphi
nēas eÿsselmous halad’ helkemen amphielissas.
sentences.l:
and he himself threatened, with dawn appearing,
to drag the well-benched ships to the sea, the both-sides-curving ones.
sentences.i: He himself threatened to drag the well-benched ships, curved on both sides, down to the sea at first light.
sentences.n: αὐτὸς δέ is ‘and he himself’, Achilles, and ἠπείλησεν takes the infinitive ἑλκέμεν (the epic form of ἕλκειν) ‘to drag’. ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι is the same formula as at 618, ‘at first light’. ἅλαδ’ is ἅλαδε ‘to the sea’ (the suffix -δε of direction); ἐϋσσέλμους ‘well-benched’ and ἀμφιελίσσας ‘curved on both sides’ (the usual reading of the word; its exact sense is uncertain) describe the ships, which are Achilles’ own.

sentences.t:
καὶ δ’ ἂν τοῖς ἄλλοισιν ἔφη παραμυθήσασθαι
οἴκαδ’ ἀποπλείειν, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι δήετε τέκμωρ
Ἰλίου αἰπεινῆς·
sentences.tr:
kai d’ an tois alloisin ephē paramythēsasthai
oikad’ apopleiein, epei ouketi dēete tekmōr
Iliou aipeinēs·
sentences.i: He said, too, that he would advise the others to sail away home, since you will no longer find an end for steep Ilios;
sentences.n: Odysseus now repeats what Achilles said at 9.417–418. ἔφη … παραμυθήσασθαι is ‘he said (he would) advise’, where ἂν keeps the ‘would’ of the direct words (ἐγὼ παραμυθησαίμην, ‘I would advise’). With οὐκέτι δήετε Odysseus slips into Achilles’ own second person: δήετε is the future of δήω ‘find’, ‘you will no longer find’. τέκμωρ is ‘an end’, and Ἰλίου αἰπεινῆς ‘of steep Ilios’; οἴκαδ’ is ‘homeward’.

sentences.t:
μάλα γάρ ἑθεν εὐρύοπα Ζεὺς
χεῖρα ἑὴν ὑπερέσχε, τεθαρσήκασι δὲ λαοί.
sentences.tr:
mala gar hethen euryopa Zeus
cheira heēn hyperesche, tetharsēkasi de laoi.
sentences.l:
for very much over it far-thundering Zeus
has held his own hand, and the people have taken courage.
sentences.i: for Zeus who thunders from afar has held his hand over it, and the troops have taken heart.
sentences.n: These are Achilles’ words of 9.419 (repeated by Odysseus). ἑθεν is the epic genitive of the pronoun, ‘of it’, with ὑπερέσχε ‘held over’ (Ilios); χεῖρα ἑὴν is ‘his own hand’, and εὐρύοπα ‘far-thundering’ is the stock epithet of Zeus. τεθαρσήκασι is the perfect of θαρσέω, ‘have taken courage’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’· εἰσὶ καὶ οἵδε τάδ’ εἰπέμεν, οἵ μοι ἕποντο,
Αἴας καὶ κήρυκε δύω πεπνυμένω ἄμφω.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’· eisi kai hoide tad’ eipemen, hoi moi heponto,
Aias kai kēryke dyō pepnymenō amphō.
sentences.l:
So he spoke; there are also these here to tell it, who followed me,
Ajax and the two heralds, the two prudent.
sentences.i: So he spoke; and here are these men too, who came with me, to say so: Ajax and the two heralds, both prudent men.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is not the narrator’s closing formula but Odysseus’ own words, ‘so he (Achilles) said’; ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο. εἰσὶ καὶ οἵδε τάδ’ εἰπέμεν is ‘there are also these here to say these things’: οἵδε ‘these here’ (the others of the embassy), εἰπέμεν the epic infinitive of εἶπον, giving their witness. οἵ μοι ἕποντο is ‘who followed me’. κήρυκε δύω πεπνυμένω ἄμφω is ‘the two heralds, both prudent men’: κήρυκε and πεπνυμένω are duals.

sentences.t:
Φοῖνιξ δ’ αὖθ’ ὃ γέρων κατελέξατο, ὡς γὰρ ἀνώγει,
ὄφρά οἱ ἐν νήεσσι φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ ἕπηται
αὔριον, ἢν ἐθέλῃσιν·
sentences.tr:
Phoinix d’ auth’ ho gerōn katelexato, hōs gar anōgei,
ophra hoi en nēessi philēn es patrid’ hepētai
aurion, ēn ethelēisin·
sentences.i: And Phoenix, the old man, lay down there in turn, for so he bade, so that he may follow him in the ships to his dear fatherland tomorrow, if he wishes;
sentences.n: This repeats Achilles’ words of 9.427–428, now in the third person. αὖθ’ is αὖτε ‘in turn’ (or αὖθι ‘there’; the free line gives both), ὃ γέρων ‘the old man’, κατελέξατο the aorist of καταλέγομαι ‘lay down’, and ὡς γὰρ ἀνώγει ‘for so he bade’ (Achilles being the subject). ὄφρα … ἕπηται is a purpose clause: ἕπηται is the subjunctive of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ with οἱ ‘him’ (Achilles) in the dative; φίλην ἐς πατρίδ’ is ‘to his dear fatherland’, Achilles’ own, and ἢν ἐθέλῃσιν ‘if he wishes’ (ἢν = ἐάν).

sentences.t: ἀνάγκῃ δ’ οὔ τί μιν ἄξει.
sentences.tr: anankēi d’ ou ti min axei.
sentences.l: but by compulsion not at all will he lead him.”
sentences.i: but he will not take him under compulsion.”
sentences.n: ἀνάγκῃ is a dative of manner, ‘by compulsion’; μιν is Phoenix, and ἄξει the future of ἄγω with Achilles as the unstated subject. Achilles said ἄξω ‘I shall not take him’ at 9.429; the person has changed, the words are the same. The end of Odysseus’ speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ
μῦθον ἀγασσάμενοι·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi
mython agassamenoi·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence,
in wonder at the speech;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent, amazed at his speech;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ … σιωπῇ is the formula ‘so he spoke, and they all became still in silence’ (also at 3.95), and it closed Achilles’ refusal in the same two lines at 9.430. ἀγασσάμενοι, from ἀγάομαι, can mean ‘be amazed at’ or ‘be indignant at’; the next unit gives the reason for the silence, and ‘amazed’ is the sense that suits it. μῦθον is the object, ‘the speech’, Odysseus’ report. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ κρατερῶς ἀγόρευσε.
sentences.tr: mala gar kraterōs agoreuse.
sentences.l: for very strongly he declared.
sentences.i: for he had declared it with great force.
sentences.n: μάλα γὰρ κρατερῶς ἀγόρευσε is the line that follows the same formula at 8.29. ἀγόρευσε is the aorist of ἀγορεύω ‘declare, speak out’, and the speaker is Odysseus, who has just finished. At 9.431 the verb was ἀπέειπεν ‘refused’, since there the speaker was Achilles.

sentences.t: δὴν δ’ ἄνεῳ ἦσαν τετιηότες υἷες Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.tr: dēn d’ aneōi ēsan tetiēotes huies Achaiōn·
sentences.l: For a long while speechless they were, grieved, the sons of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: For a long time the sons of the Achaeans were speechless, grieving;
sentences.n: δὴν ‘for a long time’ is an adverb, ἄνεῳ ‘speechless’ a plural adjective, and ἦσαν the imperfect of εἰμί; τετιηότες ‘grieving’ is a perfect participle. The same line follows the same silence after Agamemnon’s proposal of flight at 9.30, and Diomedes breaks it there too, as he does here in the next line.

sentences.t: ὀψὲ δὲ δὴ μετέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: opse de dē meteeipe boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: But late indeed spoke among them Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: At last Diomedes, good at the war-cry, spoke among them:
sentences.n: ὀψὲ δὲ δή is ‘but late, at last’, μετέειπε ‘spoke among them’, and βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ (βοήν an accusative of respect) is Diomedes’ stock epithet. The line is the same as at 9.31 and 7.399, where Diomedes also speaks after a silence.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον
μὴ ὄφελες λίσσεσθαι ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα
μυρία δῶρα διδούς·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē kydiste anax andrōn Agamemnon
mē opheles lissesthai amymona Pēleïōna
myria dōra didous·
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious Agamemnon, lord of men, would that you had not begged the blameless son of Peleus by offering countless gifts;
sentences.n: The address is the same as Odysseus’ at 677. μὴ ὄφελες … λίσσεσθαι is a wish about the past, ‘would that you had not besought’: ὄφελες is the unaugmented past of ὀφείλω used with an infinitive, and λίσσεσθαι is ‘beseech’. ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα is ‘the blameless son of Peleus’ (a patronymic, with ἀμύμων a stock epithet whose root sense is not known), and μυρία δῶρα διδούς ‘giving countless gifts’.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἀγήνωρ ἐστὶ καὶ ἄλλως·
sentences.tr: ho d’ agēnōr esti kai allōs·
sentences.l: but he is manly even otherwise;
sentences.i: he is proud enough already;
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ is ‘but he’, Achilles. ἀγήνωρ is ‘manly’ or ‘proud’ (the house rendering is ‘proud’ in the free line); with καὶ ἄλλως ‘even otherwise, in any case’ it means he was proud to begin with.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖ μιν πολὺ μᾶλλον ἀγηνορίῃσιν ἐνῆκας.
sentences.tr: nyn au min poly mallon agēnoriēisin enēkas.
sentences.l: Now again him much more into prides you have sent.
sentences.i: Now you have driven him into still greater pride.
sentences.n: ἀγηνορίῃσιν is the plural of ἀγηνορία, the abstract noun of ἀγήνωρ, ‘acts or moods of pride’, here dative after ἐνῆκας, the aorist of ἐνίημι ‘send into’. πολὺ μᾶλλον is ‘much more’, αὖ ‘again’, and μιν ‘him’. Diomedes says that Agamemnon’s offer pushed Achilles further, not nearer.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι κεῖνον μὲν ἐάσομεν ἤ κεν ἴῃσιν
ἦ κε μένῃ·
sentences.tr:
all’ ētoi keinon men easomen ē ken iēisin
ē ke menēi·
sentences.l:
But indeed that man we shall leave, whether he goes
or stays;
sentences.i: But as for him, we shall leave him alone, whether he goes or stays;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι κεῖνον μέν is ‘but as for him’ (ἤτοι is printed as one word). ἐάσομεν is ‘we shall let be’ (a future; it could also be read as a hortative subjunctive, ‘let us leave’). ἤ κεν ἴῃσιν ἦ κε μένῃ is ‘whether he goes or stays’: ἴῃσιν is the subjunctive of εἶμι with the ending -σιν, and μένῃ the subjunctive of μένω.

sentences.t:
τότε δ’ αὖτε μαχήσεται ὁππότε κέν μιν
θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀνώγῃ καὶ θεὸς ὄρσῃ.
sentences.tr:
tote d’ aute machēsetai hoppote ken min
thymos eni stēthessin anōgēi kai theos orsēi.
sentences.l:
and then in turn he will fight, whenever him
the heart in his chest bids and a god rouses.
sentences.i: he will fight again when the heart in his chest bids him and a god rouses him.
sentences.n: τότε δ’ αὖτε is ‘and then, in turn’. μαχήσεται is the future of μάχομαι, and ὁππότε κέν μιν … ἀνώγῃ … ὄρσῃ a general clause with two subjunctives, ἀνώγῃ from ἄνωγα ‘bid’ and ὄρσῃ the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. The two causes work together: his own heart (θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν) and a god.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω πειθώμεθα πάντες·
sentences.tr: all’ ageth’ hōs an egō eipō peithōmetha pantes·
sentences.l: But come, as I may say, let us obey, all of us;
sentences.i: But come, let us all do as I say;
sentences.n: Agamemnon used this line at 2.139 and again at 9.26, both times to propose flight; Diomedes now takes it for the opposite purpose. ἄγεθ’ is ἄγετε ‘come’, ὡς ἂν ἐγὼ εἴπω ‘as I may say’, and πειθώμεθα a hortative subjunctive, ‘let us obey’.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν κοιμήσασθε τεταρπόμενοι φίλον ἦτορ
σίτου καὶ οἴνοιο·
sentences.tr:
nyn men koimēsasthe tetarpomenoi philon ētor
sitou kai oinoio·
sentences.l:
Now lie down to sleep, having taken your fill in your dear heart
of food and wine;
sentences.i: Now lie down to sleep, once you have taken your fill of food and wine;
sentences.n: νῦν μέν is ‘for now’. κοιμήσασθε is the aorist imperative middle of κοιμάω ‘lie down to sleep’, and τεταρπόμενοι the aorist participle of τέρπω ‘take one’s fill’, with the genitive σίτου καὶ οἴνοιο (the epic genitive in -οιο) ‘of food and wine’. φίλον ἦτορ ‘dear heart’ is an accusative of respect, ‘in the heart’, left out of the free line.

sentences.t: τὸ γὰρ μένος ἐστὶ καὶ ἀλκή·
sentences.tr: to gar menos esti kai alkē·
sentences.l: for that is strength and might;
sentences.i: for that is strength and might;
sentences.n: τό ‘that’ is the food and wine just named; μένος ‘strength’ and ἀλκή ‘might’ are the two nouns of fighting force. The line is a saying: the meal is where fighting strength comes from.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κε φανῇ καλὴ ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
καρπαλίμως πρὸ νεῶν ἐχέμεν λαόν τε καὶ ἵππους
ὀτρύνων, καὶ δ’ αὐτὸς ἐνὶ πρώτοισι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
autar epei ke phanēi kalē rhododaktylos Ēōs,
karpalimōs pro neōn echemen laon te kai hippous
otrynōn, kai d’ autos eni prōtoisi machesthai.
sentences.l:
But when appears fair, rose-fingered Dawn,
quickly before the ships hold your people and your horses,
urging them on, and yourself fight among the first.”
sentences.i: And when fair, rose-fingered Dawn appears, quickly hold your troops and horses before the ships, urging them on, and fight yourself among the first.”
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί κε φανῇ is ‘but when … appears’ (κε with the aorist passive subjunctive of φαίνω); ῥοδοδάκτυλος ‘rose-fingered’ is the stock epithet of Dawn. ἐχέμεν and μάχεσθαι are infinitives used as imperatives (‘hold!’, ‘fight!’), and the speech turns from ‘let us’ to ‘you’, Agamemnon; ὀτρύνων is ‘urging on’. λαόν τε καὶ ἵππους is ‘people and horses’, the host and its chariots; πρὸ νεῶν ‘before the ships’; ἐνὶ πρώτοισι ‘among the first’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπῄνησαν βασιλῆες
μῦθον ἀγασσάμενοι Διομήδεος ἱπποδάμοιο.
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes epēinēsan basilēes
mython agassamenoi Diomēdeos hippodamoio.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then all approved, the kings,
in admiration at the word of Diomedes, horse-taming.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all the kings agreed, in admiration at the word of Diomedes, tamer of horses.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ closes Diomedes’ speech. ἐπῄνησαν is the aorist of ἐπαινέω ‘approve’, with the augment ἐπ-ῄ-; βασιλῆες are the kings, the chiefs in council. ἀγασσάμενοι here is ‘in admiration at’, the other sense of ἀγάομαι, as at 7.404 and unlike 693; ἱπποδάμοιο ‘horse-taming’ is the stock epithet of Diomedes, with the epic genitive -οιο.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότε δὴ σπείσαντες ἔβαν κλισίην δὲ ἕκαστος,
ἔνθα δὲ κοιμήσαντο καὶ ὕπνου δῶρον ἕλοντο.
sentences.tr:
kai tote dē speisantes eban klisiēn de hekastos,
entha de koimēsanto kai hypnou dōron helonto.
sentences.l:
And then indeed, having poured libations, they went, each to his hut,
and there they lay down to sleep and took the gift of sleep.
sentences.i: Then, when they had poured their libations, they went, each to his own hut, and there they lay down to sleep and took the gift of sleep.
sentences.n: καὶ τότε δή is ‘and then indeed’, σπείσαντες ‘having poured a libation’, and ἔβαν the aorist of βαίνω (= ἔβησαν); κλισίην δέ is ‘to the hut’ (the suffix -δε of direction), ἕκαστος ‘each’. Line 713 is the formula that ends a day: κοιμήσαντο ‘lay down to sleep’ is the aorist middle of κοιμάω, and ὕπνου δῶρον ἕλοντο ‘took the gift of sleep’ (ἕλοντο the aorist middle of αἱρέω, without augment); its second half also closes 7.482, after κοιμήσαντ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα.
